title: Start With Why
author: Simon Sinek
blurb: Simon Sinek asks why some leaders and organizations, like Apple, Southwest Airlines and Martin Luther King Junior, inspire loyalty while others with similar resources do not. His answer is a simple model he calls the Golden Circle. Most organizations communicate from the outside in. They start with what they do, then how they do it, and rarely say why. Inspiring leaders reverse the order and start with their purpose. Sinek argues this works because it speaks to the part of the brain that drives feelings and decisions. He contrasts short-term manipulation, like discounts and promotions, with lasting inspiration built on trust. He shows how a clear why attracts early believers who carry ideas into the mainstream. He also warns that organizations lose their way when growth makes the why fuzzy.

lessons.t: Why Some Leaders Inspire and Others Don't
lessons.b: Great leaders and organizations like Apple stand out not because of what they make but because they communicate their purpose first.
issues: scene 3: The laptop icon for the WHAT ring sits on the outer circle's bottom stroke, so the line cuts through the icon. (fix: Move the laptop icon inside the outer ring, in the band between the HOW and WHAT circles (for example next to or under the WHAT label), so it clears the circle stroke.)

lessons.t: The Golden Circle: Why, How, What
lessons.b: Inspiring communication moves from the inside out, starting with why, then how, then what, while most organizations do the reverse.
Price cuts, promotions, fear and novelty can drive sales, but they buy transactions rather than loyalty and grow costly over time.
The Golden Circle mirrors the brain, where the limbic system drives feelings and decisions, which is why a clear why can feel right before we can explain it.
A why only works when it is clear, guides how you act with discipline, and shows up consistently in everything you do, which builds trust.
Following the Law of Diffusion of Innovations, ideas spread when they first win the small group who share your beliefs, not when you chase the mass market directly.
issues: scene 6: The five believer figures in the inner ellipse are packed so tightly that each raised-hand stroke cuts across the neighbouring figure's head. The cluster reads as a tangled, overlapping blob instead of people raising their hands. (fix: Space the five figures about 10-15px further apart, or shrink them slightly. Draw each raised arm straight up from its own shoulder so no stroke crosses another figure.)

scene 5: The dashed arrow starts in empty space to the left of the CABLE crowd and is not attached to anything. It does not show where people are coming from, so the switch from TiVo to cable recorders is unclear. There is also a large empty gap between the sales chart and the TiVo/Cable group. (fix: Start the arrow at the TIVO box (or at a small crowd under TIVO) and curve it to the CABLE crowd. Move the TiVo/Cable group slightly left to close the gap.)

scene 3: The '0%' and '100%' axis labels above the progress bar are very small, roughly 16px at 1600 width, which is below the 18px minimum. (fix: Increase the axis label font size to at least 20px at 1600 width.)

lessons.b: As organizations grow, the why can fade into a focus on results, so leaders must keep purpose clear, as in Sinek's account of Walmart after Sam Walton.
issues: scene 7: The monospace sub-captions under each card ('SOMEONE'S REAL JOB', 'AT EVERY LEVEL', 'SHARED BELIEF, NOT JUST SKILL', 'DOES IT SERVE WHY?') render at roughly 16px at 1600 width, below the 18px minimum. (fix: Increase the card sub-caption font size to at least 18–20px. Allow two lines where needed, or widen the cards slightly so the text still fits inside them.)
